name: Apache HBase
summary: The Hadoop world’s Bigtable: huge sorted tables split into regions, each served by one RegionServer, with files kept in HDFS.
intro: An HBase table is a set of rows sorted by row key (raw bytes), with columns grouped into column families. The table is cut into regions, each a contiguous range of row keys served by exactly one RegionServer. Regions split as they grow, and the HMaster assigns and rebalances them; ZooKeeper tracks which master is active. A client looks up the region in the `hbase:meta` catalog table, then talks to that RegionServer directly. Each write is appended to the server’s write-ahead log (WAL) in HDFS, then held in the MemStore for its column family, which is later flushed to an HFile (a format based on Bigtable’s SSTable) and compacted. Because one server owns each row, reads and writes are strongly consistent and every mutation is atomic within a row, but not across rows.

That design has a cost: when a RegionServer dies, its regions can’t be read until they are reassigned and recovered, and detecting the failure alone takes 20 to 30 seconds. Rows are sorted, so sequential keys such as timestamps send every write to one region; row keys are usually salted, hashed or reversed to spread the load. You access HBase through its Java API, REST or Thrift, and Apache Phoenix adds SQL and JDBC on top. HBase is free under Apache 2.0. HBase 3.0.0 (August 2026) requires JDK 17 and drops Hadoop 2; the 2.6 and 2.5 lines still get releases. Amazon EMR runs it, optionally with its files in S3; Azure HDInsight 5.1 ships the older HBase 2.4; Google Cloud Bigtable accepts a customised HBase client.
strengths: Strongly consistent reads and writes, atomic per row, with check-and-put for compare-and-swap
Scales to billions of rows by splitting regions automatically and adding RegionServers
Rows sorted by key make scans over adjacent rows cheap
Fits the Hadoop stack: files in HDFS, and Spark, Hive, Impala and Flink can read and write tables
Code written against the HBase API can move to Google Cloud Bigtable
limits: A heavy stack to run: HDFS, ZooKeeper, HMaster and RegionServers; its own guide suggests it only for hundreds of millions of rows or more, on at least five DataNodes
When a RegionServer fails, its regions are unavailable until reassigned, and detection alone takes 20 to 30 seconds
No secondary indexes, typed columns or multi-row transactions, and a poorly chosen row key sends all traffic to one region
Its ecosystem is shrinking: Facebook moved Messenger off HBase in 2018, HDInsight still ships HBase 2.4, and Phoenix doesn’t yet support HBase 3.0
HBase 3.0 needs JDK 17, drops Hadoop 2 and puts the master in the client’s path for finding regions

sections.title: HBase or Cassandra?
sections.intro: Both store wide rows in sorted files, but they split and replicate data in opposite ways. From each project’s docs:

rows.label: Lineage
values: Bigtable: one server owns each range of rows
Dynamo plus Bigtable: equal nodes, each partition on several replicas

rows.label: Consistency
values: Strong, with atomic mutations within a row
Chosen per request; conflicting writes resolve by timestamp

rows.label: When a server fails
values: Its regions are unreadable until reassigned (detection takes 20 to 30 seconds)
Other replicas keep serving if the consistency level can still be met

rows.label: Ordering
values: Rows sorted by key across the whole table
Partitions placed by hash; rows sorted only within a partition

rows.label: Storage
values: HFiles and WAL in HDFS, or S3 on Amazon EMR
SSTables and commit log on each node’s own disks

notes: Facebook tested both in 2010 and chose HBase for Messages because of its simpler consistency model and its HDFS foundation; in 2018 it moved Messenger to MyRocks.

items.name: Self-managed
items.text: 3.0.0 for new clusters on JDK 17 and Hadoop 3, or the maintained 2.6 and 2.5 lines. You also run HDFS and ZooKeeper.

items.name: Amazon EMR
items.text: EMR 7.14.0 includes HBase 2.6.4. Since EMR 5.2.0 the HBase root directory, store files and metadata can live in S3, so clusters are sized for compute; only one cluster at a time writes to that location, plus optional read replicas.

items.name: Azure HDInsight
items.text: HDInsight 5.1 ships HBase 2.4.11 and Phoenix 5.1.2, a line the HBase project no longer lists for download. HDInsight 4.0 and 5.0 were retired on March 31, 2025; no retirement date is announced for 5.1.

items.name: Google Cloud Bigtable
items.text: Not HBase, but Google offers a customised HBase client for Java. Coprocessors, namespaces, snapshots and region management aren’t supported, since Bigtable manages its tablets itself.

story: Google’s 2006 Bigtable paper described a store of sorted rows on top of its file system. Hadoop had copied that file system as HDFS, but had no way to read and update single records in huge tables. In February 2007 Mike Cafarella posted code for “HBase, a BigTable-like file store” to Hadoop’s issue tracker. Jim Kellerman and Michael Stack, at the search start-up Powerset, took it forward as a Hadoop contrib module whose goal was a system “as similar to Google’s Bigtable as possible”. The first working version shipped with Hadoop 0.15.0 in October 2007.

HBase became a top-level Apache project in April 2010. That November Facebook chose it over MySQL and Cassandra for its new Messages system. HBase 1.0 followed in February 2015, when the ASF named Apple, Facebook, Pinterest, Salesforce, Xiaomi and Yahoo among its users.

Use has thinned since. In 2018 Facebook moved Messenger from HBase to MyRocks, to serve data from flash and fit its MySQL replication topology. Development continued: 2.0 came in 2018, and 3.0, eight years later, in August 2026.

choices.choice: Copy Bigtable rather than invent a new design
choices.why: The project’s stated goal was to stay as close to Bigtable as possible and avoid reinventing the wheel, so HFiles follow Bigtable’s SSTables and regions follow its tablets.
HDFS already gave replication, end-to-end checksums and rebalancing, so HBase didn’t need its own replication inside a cluster, and Hadoop teams already knew how to run it.

Routing all reads and writes for a row through one RegionServer orders every write and lets reads see the latest data. The price is a gap in availability while a failed server’s regions are recovered.
